Imagine playing a role in the most anticipated video game of all time — and not being able to tell a soul.
That’s the story of a graduate of St. Clair College in Windsor, Ont., whose body movements can be seen in Grand Theft Auto VI characters.

blocks.text: Preston Vendramin, 35, landed the job three years ago, but had to keep quiet until the game was released Nov. 19.
He contributed movements to Jason, one of the game’s main characters, and was key to how background characters — known as non-player characters or NPC — move and behave.
Grand Theft Auto VI was released Nov. 19. (Athit Perawongmetha/Reuters)

"It's something that's so big and so exciting, and it's something you just want to shout from the rooftops because of how exciting it is," he said. "But I knew the gravity of what I was working on, so I really had no choice but to just lock in and keep my mouth shut."

Vendramin, who now lives in Toronto and is originally from Niagara Falls, Ont., took St. Clair College’s Music Theatre Performance program between 2012 and 2015. While at school in Windsor, he performed in productions of A Chorus Line, Company, Working and Oklahoma!
Vendramin performs in a stage production of Oklahoma! (Submitted by Preston Vendramin)
More recently, he’s performed professionally in Sister Act, Who’s Under Where? and Fiddler on the Roof in Yiddish.

Vendramin, who’s an avid gamer himself, spoke with CBC Radio’s Windsor Morning host, Amy Dodge. He touched on landing the high-profile gig and what it meant to do motion capture, leaning into mundane body movements.
Here’s a portion of that conversation.
Take us back. How did you land this gig in the first place?

My agency, The Talent House, which is based out of Toronto, they sent me an audition notice. I'm like, 'OK, like I don't really know what this is,' but I had to film a series of movements, and then a couple weeks later, I got a call back to some more movements. And then a couple weeks after that, I was booked in for my first session, and the rest is history.
How does motion capture acting work? Can you take us into the studio, maybe give us what a typical day looks like?

The best way I can probably describe it: so, if you've ever seen the James Cameron's Avatar movies where they have those black suits on with the balls on them, and then the developers put that into the game.
Why birdwatchers are flocking to Grand Theft Auto VI
How sensitive are those sensors to your movements? Did you find that you needed to make larger movements or just the littlest movement would show up on the screen?
The littlest movement. They are quite sensitive.
Club dancing was a big part of the work you did. What's the strangest or maybe funniest thing you've had to do in this motion capture suit?
I don't know if it made it into the final cut, but there was a day where we were doing some dancing and I did "the worm" in the suit, but I don't know if it was able to pick it up. It was very fun.

blocks.text: OK, so the game is released. What was that night like for you?

We were allowed to talk about it. On the morning of [Nov.] 19 is when my friends and I, we made our posts and stuff like that, and the flooding of messages and notifications I got. Text messages, interviews I've had to do. It's just been an insane amount of engagement that I've never experienced before. And it's all in the spirit of curiosity. Everybody is so excited for it. That really warms my heart, that people are so genuinely congratulatory and inquisitive about my work in the game.
What's the most common question people have?

Basically, 'What did you do?' There are a lot of people that have been like, 'Oh, are you Jason?' And I'm like, 'No, I am not.' Jason is the actor Dylan Rourke, who lives in New York City. But over the course of these years, I was able to provide some body movements for the main player character. But yeah, that's something people often say, and I often have to correct them.
Were you playing the game the night it came out?
No, I was trying to beat The Legend of Zelda: The Ocarina of Time.
Vendramin is a Canadian motion capture actor in Grand Theft Auto VI. (Submitted by Preston Vendramin/David Leyes)
Zelda came out on [Nov.] 5. I wanted to beat that before I moved on to Grand Theft Auto VI.
OK, did you beat it?
No.
OK, so when do you think you'll pick up a controller for Grand Theft Auto?
I already have.

blocks.text: What was the most surreal moment for you?

Probably booting up the game for the first time and knowing that it's on my PlayStation. It's real. It's tangible, and I'm finally getting to delve into the world that so many people have waited 13 years for.
A gamer plays Grand Theft Auto VI on Nov. 19. (Athit Perawongmetha/Reuters)
It sounds as though it was exciting to play. What was it like to see your work in the video game?
Very cool for me, and it's very cool for my friends that I can talk about it with them.
Are you seeing movement in real life differently now?

Oh yeah. And not only do I look at the movement in the game differently, I also look at people's movements in real life differently because that's what ultimately they are after for the game is not overly exaggerated stuff, but just real people. It's very cool to watch.

blocks.text: Is there anything that you have noticed that you wouldn't have noticed before?

People’s very small idiosyncrasies that they have when they sit down. They don't just sit down, they sit down and they have like a small breath or a sigh or something. That's what makes it real. Those moments in between, which I think are so cool.
A gamer plays GTA VI the day it was released earlier this month. (Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters)
